note.headline: Strong bounce day, but SPY and QQQ remain below their 50-day averages

summary.thesis: The long-term uptrend still holds for both indices, but the short-term trend is broken. Only 25% of stocks sit above their own 50-day average, while fear is in the 'normal' range.
summary.decision: Be selective. The long-term picture is intact, but most stocks are not taking part, and QQQ still fails the pipeline's 'above its 50-day average' market check.
summary.act_at: QQQ close above 718.87 (50-day average) to lean in more; QQQ close below 680.65 or SPY close below 728.65 (200-day averages) to stand aside.

note.happening: On 2026-11-11, SPY closed at 759.81, up 1.32% from 749.92. QQQ closed at 690.38, up 2.31% from 674.76. The rally came after a pullback: both indices set 1-month closing lows on Nov 5 (SPY 733.0, QQQ 647.05). Over 20 trading days SPY is still down 1.27% and QQQ is down 5.29%. Over 5 days they are down 0.91% and 0.23%. Both remain under the past year's highest closes of 779.09 (SPY) and 759.66 (QQQ), both set on Oct 6. The VIX fear gauge fell from about 19.46 to about 17.49. No news has been reported since the last note. Coming up: PPI producer-price data on Nov 13 at 08:30, and NVDA earnings, with an estimated date of Nov 17 after the close.
note.business: Trend: both indices are labeled 'sideways'. Each is above its 200-day average (SPY 728.65, QQQ 680.65), so the long trend holds. Each is below its 50-day average (SPY 764.55, QQQ 718.87), so the short trend is broken. SPY is only 0.6% below its 50-day line, while QQQ is 4.1% below its own, so tech is the weaker part. Fear: the VIX is in the 'normal' 15–20 band, at the 56th percentile of its past 252 days. Investors are not panicking, and they are not complacent either. Breadth: 25% of stocks are above their 50-day average. Together, these readings point to a market that is calm on the surface but narrow underneath. The index bounce is not yet matched by most individual stocks. (General knowledge: narrow participation often makes index gains less durable until more stocks join in.) The pipeline's market gate is not active.

worth.text: DATA has no valuation inputs (earnings, multiples or yields) for SPY or QQQ, so this note makes no fair-value estimate. The only reference points are the price levels in the trend gates.
worth.key_assumption: No valuation is implied. The levels cited are trend references, not estimates of worth.

bull: Both SPY and QQQ remain above their 200-day averages (728.65 and 680.65), so the long-term trend counts as up.
The Nov 5 one-month lows (SPY 733.0, QQQ 647.05) are holding, and Nov 11 brought a strong bounce: SPY +1.32%, QQQ +2.31%.
Fear is 'normal': the VIX fell to about 17.49 from about 19.46, at the 56th percentile of its past year.
bear: Both indices sit below their 50-day averages, so the short-term trend is broken. QQQ is 4.1% below its 50-day line at 718.87.
Breadth is weak: only 25% of stocks are above their 50-day average, so the rally is narrow.
QQQ is down 5.29% over 20 days and sits 5.6% below its 1-month high of 728.95. NVDA earnings (estimated Nov 17) could move the whole tech group either way.

SPY 1-month high (Oct 21): a close above it would mean SPY's pullback is fully recovered.

SPY 1-month low (Nov 5): a close below it would mean the decline is continuing.

QQQ 200-day average: a close below it would put tech's long-term trend down. That would be a stand-aside signal.

note.headline: Tesla trades near the top of its own history while profits shrink

summary.thesis: Tesla has a strong balance sheet, but the 390.84 price needs far faster growth than the shrinking margins and cash flow now show.
summary.decision: Long-term: avoid. Swing: wait, because the price sits just under resistance with no clear trend.
summary.act_at: Revisit near 203.8 on value; watch 380.15–400.51 for the trading range

note.happening: TSLA closed at 390.84, up 2.91% on the day. That puts it just under a resistance band at 393.63–400.51 and near its 20-, 50- and 200-day averages (381.83, 373.65, 383.03), which are all flat, so the stock is moving sideways. There is no news since the last note, and the next earnings report is on 2027-01-27.
note.business: The latest quarter (ended 2026-09-30, filed 2026-10-22) weakened the business. Quarterly sales fell 0.17% from a year earlier, down from 15.78% growth two quarters ago. Operating margin, the share of sales left after running costs, slipped to 3.35% from 4.74%. Trailing free cash flow, the cash left after spending, halved to 3.3B from 6.8B. Inventory is up 15% while quarterly sales are up 0% (both against a year earlier). That gap can force price cuts and squeeze margins again. The quality grade is D. Not at risk is the balance sheet: 17.9B cash against 8.0B debt, 37.5B net cash and 45.4B total liquidity, so funding stress is not the issue. Share dilution is small at 0.43% a year. The rally to 390.84 reflects sentiment more than results. Segment data is not available, so this note cannot say which product lines drive the slowdown.

worth.text: The two valuation methods disagree sharply. A cash-flow valuation (DCF) starts from 3.3B of trailing free cash flow and a 9.9% discount rate. It gives 20.23 (bear), 25.02 (base) and 45.34 (bull) per share. Even with 30% starting growth it reaches only 45.55, and if operating margin falls to 1% it drops to 21.83. The second method asks what the stock would be worth at its usual price-to-sales ratios over the past 5 years, and gives 203.8 to 399.81. The price is 430.1 times trailing earnings and 14.9 times sales, at the 77th percentile of its own 5-year price-to-sales range. The data estimates that the price needs about 51% a year growth, while sales grew 3% a year over 3 years and 8% over the last 12 months. The gap between the methods comes down to one assumption: whether investors keep paying a high sales multiple for growth the cash flows do not yet show. My range uses the history-based values. The cash-flow values sit far below them.
worth.key_assumption: The market keeps valuing Tesla within its own 5-year price-to-sales range rather than on current free cash flow.

bull: The balance sheet is strong: 37.5B net cash and 45.4B liquidity give room to invest through a slow patch.
Trailing sales still grew to 103.6B from 95.6B, and analysts' next-year EPS growth is 25%.
The price sits above its 50-day average of 373.65, with heavy support at 380.15–389.95 (11 touches).
bear: The price is 430.1 times trailing earnings, and every cash-flow value is at or below 45.34 per share.
Free cash flow halved to 3.3B from 6.8B, and operating margin fell to 3.35% from 4.74%.
Inventory is up 15% while quarterly sales are up 0%, which signals possible price cuts ahead.

levels.what: The current close, near the top of the history-based range and far above every cash-flow value.
The top of the own-history price-to-sales range. Above this, even the generous method calls the stock expensive.
The low end of the own-history range, where the price would start to reflect slower growth.

longterm.why: This is a grade D business with falling margins and cash flow, priced near the top of its own valuation history. The rules committee also says Avoid.

swing.why: The stock is in a sideways range, just under resistance at 393.63–400.51 and above support at 380.15–389.95. The room to the next ceiling is small next to the 16.61 average daily range. A clear close above 400.51 or a pullback into support would give a better setup.

decision.timing: Earnings come out on 2027-01-27, after the 2027-01-15 options expiry. Options price only about a 5.5% move by 2026-11-20 (implied volatility 42.5 vs realized 61.3), so the big catalyst is the January report, not the coming weeks.

change_mind: The 2027-01-27 report shows operating margin back above 4.74% and the inventory build easing against sales.
Trailing free cash flow recovers toward 6.8B, which would lift the cash-flow values from the 20.23–45.34 range.
A close below the 364.02–368.6 support zone would confirm weakness, and a close above 417.44 would break the range upward.

note.headline: NVIDIA: CEO exit confirmed before earnings; strong business at a low-end price

summary.thesis: The business is growing faster and earning more cash than a year ago, and the price sits near the low end of fair value; the open questions are leadership and the earnings report on 2026-11-17.
summary.decision: Long-term hold, with no new money before earnings; no swing trade until the report is out.

note.happening: NVIDIA closed at 173.73, up 2.87% on the day. An intraday reading of 164.74 (not a close) puts the stock inside its only support zone of 162.81–164.98. NVIDIA announced a CEO transition, and an 8-K filing confirms a change in its officers. Earnings arrive on 2026-11-17, and options are pricing a 9.9% move by the 2026-11-20 expiry.
note.business: The numbers in the latest quarter (ended 2026-07-26) show a business that is speeding up, not slowing down. Sales growth versus a year earlier rose from 73.21% two quarters ago to 105.85%. Trailing revenue is 303.0B, up from 165.2B. Operating margin, the share of sales left after running costs, rose to 65.21% from 58.09%. Free cash flow, the cash left after investment, is 127.0B, up from 72.0B, and the company holds 23.2B more cash than debt. None of that is changed by this week's news. The CEO transition and a board probe of Jensen Huang (reported; the company hired an outside prosecutor to lead it, reported) are governance events. They change sentiment now. They could affect strategy and key customer relationships later (general knowledge), but nothing in DATA shows that yet. The real business risks are elsewhere. Unpaid customer bills grew 127% while sales grew 106%, which can mean sales were pulled forward or customers are stretched. A 65% operating margin sits at the top of its 5-year range of 16–65%. Insiders also sold $946.6M outside pre-set plans. Demand and cash are not at risk on today's data. Margins and the quality of receivables are the parts to watch.

worth.text: On earnings, the stock trades at 21.9 times the last year and 10.9 times next year's analyst estimate. On sales it trades at 13.8 times, below the peer median of 17.1 and at the 9th percentile of its own 5-year history. The cash-flow model (DCF, which values future cash in today's money) gives 195.92 / 228.42 / 272.22 for bear, base and bull. The price-to-sales history method gives 217.35 to 411.04. The DCF caps starting growth at 30%, so the gap between bear and bull comes mainly from the discount rate (9.9%, plus or minus 1 point). The bigger gap, between the DCF and the history method, comes from assuming the stock earns its past sales multiples again. Today's price implies free cash flow growth of about 22.7% to start, then fading. At 20% starting growth the value is 156.62; at 30% it is 228.42. The real swing factor is margin. If operating margin fell to 48%, the value drops to 117.71. My range is 156.62 to 228.42, and the price sits in the lower half of it.
worth.key_assumption: Free cash flow starts growing at 20–30% a year and operating margin stays near today's 65%, not back toward 48%.

bull: Cheap against peers and its own past: price-to-sales of 13.8 compares with a peer median of 17.1 and sits at the 9th percentile of its 5-year range.
Growth is speeding up: quarterly sales growth went from 73.21% to 105.85%, and free cash flow rose to 127.0B from 72.0B.
Analysts' next-year EPS estimate of 15.91 rose 23.9% over 90 days, which puts the stock at 10.9 times next year's earnings.
bear: Margins may be at a peak: operating margin of 65% is the top of its 5-year range, and at a 48% margin the model value falls to 117.71.
Receivables grew 127% against sales growth of 106%, which can mean sales were pulled forward.
The chart is weak: the price is in a downtrend below its falling 50-day average of 217.1, while the CEO changes and a probe (reported) run into earnings.

levels.what: Today's close, in the lower half of the 156.62–228.42 fair-value range; enough to hold, not urgent enough to add before earnings.
Bottom of the only support zone (162.81–164.98); an area to add after earnings if the margin and receivables data hold up.
Base-case DCF value; near here the valuation upside is used up and it is time to reassess.

longterm.why: The automated rule says buy and the committee says hold. With a confirmed CEO change, a reported probe and earnings days away, holding respects both a strong business and a cloudy near term.

swing.why: The stock is in a downtrend, with resistance at 175.15–179.53 (4 touches) sitting just above the close. Earnings fall inside the window, and the 9.9% implied move against an ATR (average daily range) of 8.7 means a report can gap straight through any stop.

decision.timing: Wait for the 2026-11-17 report. Option prices show implied volatility of 74.4 against 52.8 realized, so a big move is expected. Act after the report shows whether margins and receivables hold.

change_mind: Bearish: a close below 162.81 (support breaks), or an earnings report showing operating margin falling back toward 58.09% or below.
Bearish: analysts cut the next-year EPS estimate of 15.91, or receivables keep growing faster than sales.
Bullish: a close above 185.22 (top of the upper resistance zone) would break the pattern of lower highs and support adding toward 195.92.

note.headline: AMD: fast growth and rising margins, but the price runs far past value

summary.thesis: AMD's business is getting stronger fast, but at 552.9 the price already assumes years of growth well beyond what any of our valuation methods support.
summary.decision: Long-term: wait, with no new buying at these levels. Swing: wait, because the price sits in the middle of its range just under resistance.
summary.act_at: Revisit near 480.33–502.6 support; value case only near 333.38 or below

note.happening: AMD closed at 552.9. It traded at 576.7 intraday (as of 10:54 ET, not a close), up 7.32% on the day, which takes it into the 574.2–596.07 resistance zone. There is no news in our data since the last note. The next earnings report is on 2027-02-02.
note.business: Business facts: demand is speeding up. Sales grew 44.68% from a year earlier in the latest quarter, compared with 37.85% two quarters ago. Trailing revenue is 45.4B, up from 32.0B. Profitability is improving too. Operating margin (profit from operations per dollar of sales) rose to 17.72% from 8.78%, and free cash flow (cash left after running and investing in the business) rose to 7.1B from 5.4B. The balance sheet is not at risk: net cash is 8.7B and liquidity is 15.8B. Analysts are raising their numbers: next-year EPS (earnings per share) estimates are up 12.1% in 30 days. What is at risk: inventory grew 57% while quarterly sales grew 45%. Unsold product can lead to price cuts. And the 17.72% operating margin sits near the top of its 5-year range of -2% to 22%, a level that often fades. Dilution is modest at 1.22% a year, and stock pay (SBC) is 4.4% of revenue. Today's 7.32% jump has no news behind it in our data, so it changes sentiment, not the business.

worth.text: At 552.9 the price is above every valuation method we have. Our discounted cash flow model (DCF: today's value of future cash) gives 148.51 / 190.99 / 226.75 for bear / base / bull. The model caps starting growth at 30%. Even at that cap the value is 190.99, and at 20% growth it is 132.38. Pricing AMD by its own past price-to-sales gives 179.24–333.38. The stock trades at 20.0 times sales, compared with a peer median of 14.7, and sits at the 93rd percentile of its own 5-year range. The gap comes down to one input: the DCF caps growth at 30%, but analysts expect next-year EPS growth of 119%. If that happens, next year's P/E (price divided by earnings) is 31.3, far below today's trailing 120.5. Margins matter too. If operating margin fell to 13%, the model value would drop to 100.61.
worth.key_assumption: The price only makes sense if analysts' forecast of a jump to 17.69 EPS next year comes true and earnings keep growing beyond the 30% the model allows.

bull: Growth is speeding up: quarterly sales grew 44.68% from a year earlier, compared with 37.85% two quarters ago.
Margins nearly doubled: operating margin rose to 17.72% from 8.78%, and free cash flow reached 7.1B.
Analysts keep raising forecasts: next-year EPS of 17.69 is up 12.1% in 30 days, which would bring the forward P/E down to 31.3.
bear: Valuation is stretched: the price of 552.9 is above the full fair-value range of 148.51–333.38, and the trailing P/E is 120.5.
Inventory rose 57% while sales rose 45%, a possible early sign of future price cuts.
Operating margin of 17.72% is near its 5-year peak of 22%. If it fell to 13%, the model value would drop to 100.61.

Top of the 480.33–502.6 support zone (5 touches). This is a better entry if the business keeps beating expectations.
Top of the fair-value range (own-history price-to-sales high). This is where the valuation case begins.

note.headline: Amazon trades at the top of its value range while cash burn deepens

summary.thesis: Amazon is growing and its margins are widening, but it is burning cash and its price already sits at the top of its own historical value range, so there is little room for error.
summary.decision: Long-term: wait for a lower price. Swing: wait; there is no clean setup between support and resistance.
summary.act_at: Near 238.65 (mid value), or 251.93–257.04 support if the business improves

note.happening: Amazon closed at 266.17, down 1.74% on the day. It was trading at 269.26 at 10:54 ET, which is not a close. The stock is in a downtrend but still sits above its 20-, 50- and 200-day averages (255.87, 254.41, 244.35), and all three averages are flat. The news is minor. Ring reportedly launched a home-security drone and a security robot for businesses, and a former AWS cloud executive was reported as the next infrastructure head at Meta. No earnings date is in the data.
note.business: Several things are changing the business itself. Sales keep growing, with trailing 12-month revenue of 797.5B against 691.3B a year earlier. But growth is slowing: the latest quarter grew 12.09% from a year earlier, against 16.61% two quarters ago. Profitability is improving. Operating margin (profit from operations per dollar of sales) rose to 13.09% from 11.02%. Cash is the problem. Free cash flow (cash left after spending on operations and investment) was -46.9B over 12 months, against +10.6B a year earlier. That pushed Amazon to net debt of 66.7B (net cash of -66.7B). Heavy spending on data centers is the usual explanation for this kind of cash drain (general knowledge). The filings also flag unpaid customer bills up 61% while quarterly sales rose 12%. That can mean sales are being pulled forward or customers are paying more slowly. What is not at risk: liquidity (cash plus credit it can draw on) of 114.2B covers near-term needs, and share dilution is small at 0.77% a year. The Ring launches and the Meta hire change sentiment and headlines, not the numbers.

worth.text: There is no discounted-cash-flow value (a value built from projected future cash), because free cash flow is negative. The only method left compares price to sales against Amazon's own last 5 years. That gives 187.93 at the cheap end, 238.65 in the middle and 266.17 at the expensive end. Today's price equals the top of that range, and price-to-sales sits at the 80th percentile of its own 5-year history. Against earnings, the stock trades at 21.6 times trailing earnings and 20.8 times this year's estimate. It is 24.9 times next year's, because analysts expect next-year earnings per share of 10.67, below this year's 12.8. The filings note that the price needs about 34% a year growth, against 13% a year delivered over 3 years. The gap between the views comes down to the yardstick. Against its own history Amazon looks fully priced. Against peers it looks cheap, with price-to-sales of 3.6 against a peer median of 6.7 and a growth-adjusted ratio of 0.61 against peers.
worth.key_assumption: Amazon's price-to-sales stays within its own 5-year range rather than moving toward the higher peer median.

bull: Operating margin rose to 13.09% from 11.02%, so each dollar of sales now produces more operating profit.
Price-to-sales of 3.6 is well below the peer median of 6.7, and the growth-adjusted ratio of 0.61 against peers also points to cheap.
Next-year earnings estimates rose 1.4% over the last 30 days, and liquidity of 114.2B leaves room to keep investing.
bear: Free cash flow swung to -46.9B from +10.6B a year earlier, leaving net debt of 66.7B.
Quarterly revenue growth slowed to 12.09% from 16.61% two quarters ago, while the price needs about 34% a year growth.
Unpaid customer bills rose 61% while sales rose 12%, and next-quarter earnings estimates were cut 2.6% over 30 days.

levels.what: Today's close, equal to the top of the value range. Not a level to add at.
Bottom of the strongest support zone (251.93–257.04, 6 touches). A better entry if cash flow stabilises.
Midpoint of the own-history value range, where price and fair value meet.

longterm.why: The business is improving on margins but burning cash, and the price already reflects the top of its value range. The rule-based verdict is 'Too expensive', with a committee call of 'Avoid'.

swing.why: The trend is down and the price sits between support at 258.08–263.7 and resistance at 274.75–278.56, so a stop and a target give poor balance. Realized volatility (42.4) is above implied volatility (33.4), so recent swings have been larger than options are pricing.

decision.timing: No earnings date is in the data; options to 2026-11-20 price a move of about 4.3%, so a test of 258.08–263.7 support is the next point to reassess.

change_mind: Free cash flow over 12 months turning positive again (against -46.9B now), which would allow a cash-flow-based valuation.
A daily close below 251.93 would break the strongest support. A close above 278.56 would clear the first resistance and challenge the downtrend.
Quarterly revenue growth back to 16.61% or higher from 12.09%, alongside unpaid customer bills growing more slowly than the 61% now flagged.
note.label: Research, not advice.

note.headline: Microsoft's profits are strong, but its cash flow trails the price; hold

summary.thesis: Microsoft is a high-quality business with faster sales growth and wider margins, but heavy spending has cut its free cash flow, and the price already assumes that spending pays back.
summary.decision: Hold for the long term and wait for a lower price before adding; no swing trade from the middle of the range.

note.happening: MSFT closed at 521.13, down 2.26% on the day, and is trading sideways between support at 504.96–512.76 and resistance at 539.31–543.27. The intraday price of 525.14 at 10:54 ET is not a close. The only news is The Verge's report that Microsoft's DLSS competitor (an upscaling feature for games) is out for the Xbox Ally X. The next earnings report is due on 2027-01-27.
note.business: The core business is getting stronger. Quarterly sales growth rose to 18.8% from 18.3% two quarters ago. The operating margin (profit from operations per dollar of sales) widened to 47.1% from 46.27%. Analysts have raised next-year earnings per share by 2.2% over the last 30 days. Cash is the weak spot. Trailing free cash flow, the cash left after spending on buildings and equipment, fell to 60.0B from 78.0B, and the free cash flow margin is only 17.31%. The company's filings flag that each dollar invested now earns 30¢ a year, against 51¢ three years ago. Put simply, the heavy spending is not paying back yet. That is the real business risk, and it is about returns, not demand. The balance sheet is safe, with net cash of 29.0B, and the share count is shrinking slightly (-0.27% a year). The Xbox news affects sentiment only. It does not change demand, margins or cash in any way the data shows. The annual report adds 4 new risk headings. The filing summary describes them as worth reading but not alarming.

worth.text: The methods disagree sharply. A discounted cash flow model (DCF), which values the company on the cash it generates, gives 184.7 / 223.82 / 296.75 for the bear, base and bull cases. Its starting point is the depressed 60.0B of free cash flow. For today's price to make sense on that model, free cash flow would need to start growing at about 40.9% a year. The model caps starting growth at 30%, and even that cap gives only 352.37. On its own history, the stock's price-to-sales ratio implies 475.73 / 535.43 / 592.92, and the stock sits at the 40th percentile of its own 5-year range. On earnings, it trades at 27.2 times trailing earnings and 21.5 times next year's. Against peers it looks expensive: 11.2 times sales against a peer median of 4.1. The gap between the methods comes down to one question: is today's free cash flow temporarily low because of an investment cycle, or is it the new normal? I side with the history-based range because earnings and margins are still rising. That view holds only if the spending pays back. If it does not, the DCF range is the honest anchor.
worth.key_assumption: The heavy spending that cut free cash flow from 78.0B to 60.0B turns back into cash, so earnings (EPS 19.16 trailing, 24.2 expected next year) rather than today's cash flow are the right basis for value.

bull: Growth is speeding up, not slowing: quarterly sales growth is 18.8%, against 18.3% two quarters ago.
Profitability is improving: the operating margin rose to 47.1% from 46.27%.
Earnings expectations are rising: next-year EPS estimates are up 2.2% in 30 days, putting the stock at 21.5 times next year's earnings.
bear: Cash generation fell: trailing free cash flow dropped to 60.0B from 78.0B.
Spending returns are shrinking: each invested dollar earns 30¢ a year, against 51¢ three years ago.
The price is demanding: it implies 40.9% starting cash-flow growth, the DCF base value is 223.82, and price-to-sales is 11.2 against a peer median of 4.1.

levels.what: Today's close sits inside the fair range of 475.73–535.43, so there is no reason to sell and no margin of safety for new money.
The top of the strongest support zone (486.0–491.22, tested 8 times) is where adding gets more attractive.
The top of the upper resistance zone. Above it, the price nears the own-history high of 592.92 and the case for trimming grows.

Meta trades at 6.7 times sales, close to the peer median of 6.5 and at the 38th percentile of its own past five years. Its price is 21.5 times trailing earnings. Operating margin, the share of each sales dollar left after running costs, edged up to 33.32% from 32.19%. The real worry is cash. The balance sheet is not at risk: net cash is 139.0B and liquidity is 265.1B. worth.text: The methods disagree sharply, and one assumption explains most of the gap. The cash-flow model (DCF) starts from free cash flow of only 19.7B and gives 26.28 / 52.56 / 72.2 per share. Even at 30% starting growth it reaches only 80.15. On that basis the price looks far too high: the filings-based risk note says the price needs about 37% a year growth, against 17% a year delivered over 3 years. But that earnings figure is inflated by the gap between net and operating margin, and the next-year multiple rises to 19.6. I treat the own-history range as the usable anchor and discount the DCF, because its cash base sits at a low point caused by heavy spending.
worth.key_assumption: Free cash flow recovers from 19.7B toward the prior 73.6B once AI spending pays off. If it stays near 19.7B, even the 234.35 low is generous.

worth.text: On today's earnings MU looks cheap: 10.9 times trailing earnings, and 6.9 times sales against a peer median of 8.6. But those earnings come from a peak year. The model gives no full discounted-cash-flow value, because a one-year jump from 1.7B to 59.0B in free cash flow can't be projected forward.
